newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Patriarch unhappy at Yeltsin veto of religion bill.
newsitem.headline: Patriarch unhappy at Yeltsin veto of religion bill.

text.p: In a rare spat between church and state, Russia's senior clergyman on Thursday criticised President Boris Yeltsin's veto of a controversial law on religion and accused the bill's foreign opponents of hypocrisy.

Patriarch Alexiy, head of the influential Orthodox Church, said in a statement that Yeltsin's veto of the draft law "On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Associations" risked stirring up religious tensions in Russia.

"The decision of the president has evoked regret among believers of the Russian Orthodox Church," said the statement, which was read out at a news conference near the patriarch's Moscow residence by Archbishop Sergiy of Solnechnogorsk.
"(The veto) could create tensions in Russia between the authorities and a majority of the people," it said.
Yeltsin threw out the bill on Tuesday, saying it contravened Russia's post-Soviet constitution guaranteeing equality for all confessions and also its international pledges on human rights.

The bill, strongly backed by his communist and nationalist opponents in parliament, had stirred fears among human rights groups and minority religious groups that Russia was returning to Soviet-style state control of worship.
The United States and Pope John Paul II had also expressed concern for religious freedom in Russia.

The patriarch said in his statement that the bill would not have curtailed the rights of Roman Catholics, Protestants and other minority confessions but was aimed at controlling a post-communist explosion in religious sects in Russia.
Many countries had laws restricting the activities of such sects, his statement said. "(Foreign opposition to the bill) speaks of biased attitudes and double standards towards Russia."

Russia's 1,000-year-old Orthodox Church is jealous of its central role in the country's history and has been alarmed by the spread of diverse religious groups on its home turf since the fall of atheistic communism.

But the church, avidly wooed in recent years by politicians of every hue -- including Yeltsin -- trying to benefit from its spiritual authority and colourful symbolism, usually steers clear of political controversy.

"The church is not a political force in society and is not linked to any political party. We do not represent the opposition," Metropolitan Kiril of Smolensk and Kaliningrad told Thursday's news conference.

"But there are questions on which the church cannot be silent," he said, underlining its role as the nation's moral guardian. "We must speak the truth to our people, our government and our president."
The bearded Kiril was flanked by two other senior Orthodox clergymen in flowing black robes, Mufti Ravil Gainutdin of Russia's Islamic community and the Buddhists' Lama Dashi-Nyama Garmazapov.

The bill had recognised Orthodoxy, Islam, Buddhism and Judaism as Russia's traditional religions. The Moslem and Buddhist representatives echoed their Orthodox colleagues' dismay about Yeltsin's veto.
"We have to approve this bill," said the shaven-headed Garmazapov, who wore the maroon robes of the Tibetan school of Buddhism that is dominant in Russia.
"Why all this noise, all this interest from abroad? Surely we have the right in Russia to order our affairs as we wish?"
Archbishop Sergiy said the traditional faiths such as Orthodoxy lacked the cash to compete with the new sects that have sprung up in Russia, often with strong foreign financial backing.

The patriarch said in his statement that he hoped the bill, which now goes back to parliament for reconsideration, would still be approved in substance. Both houses of parliament need a two-thirds majority to override Yeltsin's veto.
